candidates.attacker_control: The attacker fully controls the JSON document (e.g., an HTTP request body parsed by the application with JSON.parse / JSON.parseObject(String) / JSON.parseObject(text, Object.class) or any value whose declared type is Object, a Map, an interface or an abstract class). The `@type` string selects any class loadable from the application/JDK classpath; the remaining keys/values control the constructor path and the setter arguments invoked on the instantiated object (e.g., dataSourceName, autoCommit for JdbcRowSetImpl).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: (1) A deny mechanism does exist and is actually enforced before deserializer creation (ParserConfig lines 360-367) - but the default denyList contains only "java.lang.Thread" (line 147) and can only be extended locally via -Dfastjson.parser.deny or addDeny(), so JDK/library gadget classes are not blocked. (2) Type-constrained paths do limit the attack: JavaBeanDeserializer lines 533-559 require `expectClass.isAssignableFrom(userType)` and otherwise throw "type not match", so applications that parse only into fixed concrete bean types with no Object/interface fields are much less exposed; untyped APIs (JSON.parse, JSON.parseObject(String)) remain fully exposed via the Map path. (3) Feature.DisableSpecialKeyDetect would neutralize the `@type` handling, but it is not part of DEFAULT_PARSER_FEATURE (JSON.java lines 91-103) and no application-level enabling exists in this source tree. (4) No autoType gate exists to counterbalance the finding: case-insensitive search for "autotype" over the whole readable tree returns zero hits, and neither checkAutoType nor autoTypeSupport/SuuportAutoType symbols exist (relation index find_symbols returns nothing for checkAutoType).
candidates.impact: Remote code execution in the affected JVM when a gadget is reachable (the well-known fastjson <=1.2.24 autoType RCE, CVE-2017-18349), or at minimum attacker-driven arbitrary class instantiation plus reflective property assignment on any loadable class (CWE-502), allowing denial of service, SSRF/JNDI interactions, file/system-property side effects and, in many deployments, full compromise. Any service that feeds untrusted JSON to fastjson without a concrete target type is exposed.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) Application parses untrusted JSON with fastjson and the entry point does not force a concrete target class (untyped parse, Object/Map/interface target, or a compatible declared supertype so the JavaBeanDeserializer assignability check at lines 553-559 passes). 2) A usable gadget class exists on the classpath/JDK - canonical 2017 fastjson payloads rely on com.sun.rowset.JdbcRowSetImpl (JDK <= 8u191-style environments where JNDI remote codebase loading is allowed) or other side-effect setters/classes. 3) For remote code execution, the process can reach an attacker-controlled LDAP/RMI/JNDI endpoint, or an in-classpath gadget chain provides the effect.
candidates.root_cause: The parser treats the JSON key `@type` as a fully trusted class selector. In src/main/java/com/alibaba/fastjson/parser/DefaultJSONParser.java (parseObject(Map,Object), lines 320-368) no autoType enablement/whitelist check precedes `TypeUtils.loadClass(typeName, config.getDefaultClassLoader())` (line 322); the loaded class is passed straight to `config.getDeserializer(clazz)` (lines 334/367) and `deserializer.deserialze(...)` (line 368). There is no `ParserConfig.checkAutoType`/`autoTypeSupport` and no `Feature.SupportAutoType` anywhere in the repository (also absent from the P1 relation index), so autoType is always effectively on. `TypeUtils.loadClass` (util/TypeUtils.java lines 995-1051) resolves any name via the supplied classloader, the thread context classloader, or `Class.forName`, with no allow/deny filtering. The only guard is the denyList check in `ParserConfig.getDeserializer(Class,Type)` (parser/ParserConfig.java lines 360-367), but the default denyList is just `{"java.lang.Thread"}` (line 147, seeded at line 263) plus the empty-by-default `fastjson.parser.deny` system property (lines 122-124, 288-291; test resource src/test/resources/fastjson.properties line 6 sets it empty). Gadget classes (e.g., com.sun.rowset.JdbcRowSetImpl, TemplatesImpl, etc.) therefore pass. After instantiation, `JavaBeanDeserializer` creates the object and default field deserialization writes attacker values through setters: `FieldDeserializer.setValue` invokes `method.invoke(object, value)` (parser/deserializer/FieldDeserializer.java line 96) / `FieldInfo.set` (util/FieldInfo.java lines 458-465), executing gadget setter side effects.
candidates.title: Untrusted @type autoType deserialization enables arbitrary class instantiation and gadget-based code execution (missing checkAutoType/autoType gate)
candidates.trace: JSON.parse/parseObject (JSON.java lines 127-144, 196-204) -> DefaultJSONParser.parse()/parse(Object) (lines 1292-1327: LBRACE -> parseObject(JSONObject,...)) -> DefaultJSONParser.parseObject(Map,Object) line 320 `key == JSON.DEFAULT_TYPE_KEY` (default parser features do NOT include DisableSpecialKeyDetect; see JSON.java lines 91-103) -> line 322 `TypeUtils.loadClass(typeName, config.getDefaultClassLoader())` (TypeUtils.java lines 995-1051; classLoader/contextClassLoader/Class.forName) -> line 367 `config.getDeserializer(clazz)` -> ParserConfig.getDeserializer(Class,Type) line 327, deny check lines 360-367 (default list only "java.lang.Thread"), then createJavaBeanDeserializer line 461 -> JavaBeanDeserializer instantiation/field loop -> FieldDeserializer.setValue line 96 `method.invoke(object, value)` (FieldInfo.set lines 458-465) -> gadget setter executes (e.g., JdbcRowSetImpl.setAutoCommit -> connect() -> InitialContext.lookup(dataSourceName) -> remote class load). Note: the relation index confirms getDeserializer -> createJavaBeanDeserializer as a syntactic call candidate and contains no checkAutoType symbol.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed, built, or run - this is static source evidence only, and I did not create or run any exploit payload or JNDI endpoint. I did not verify at runtime that a specific gadget (JdbcRowSetImpl/TemplatesImpl) works on the deployment's JDK, that remote JNDI codebase loading is permitted, or that the consuming application exposes an untyped parse entry point; those are usage/JDK-dependent. In addition, the relation index provides no data-flow/control-flow and no reachability proof, so the call path is established from source text, not from dynamic analysis. I did not inspect every one of the ~2034 Java files in depth (ASM codegen, serializer package, support/* integrations were only sampled).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-502 Deserialization of Untrusted Data (unsafe polymorphic/autoType deserialization)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 2092 root files, 2091 model-visible after safety filters (1 file excluded by sensitive-name/path policy, 0 symlinks, 0 over-5MiB exclusions; binary-like files are refused/skipped). The tree is fastjson 1.2.25-SNAPSHOT: ~2034 Java files (main + tests) plus RFC 4627 text. I reviewed in depth the JSON entry points (JSON.java), the parser core (DefaultJSONParser, JSONLexerBase/JSONScanner sampled), parser config/Feature, TypeUtils class loading, and the deserializer path (JavaBeanDeserializer/FieldDeserializer/MapDeserializer/ThrowableDeserializer/MiscCodec) and sampled the test suite for security-context tests (DenyTest 1-3, TypeUtils tests, @type tests). P1 relation scope: index status partial; parsed 1892 of 2034 Java files, 27 omitted files, 29,211 symbols, 52,297 edges, with explicit gaps: no control-flow, no data-flow, no semantic resolution, and 24,443 unresolved calls - coverage is navigational only and no unreported area should be assumed reviewed. I did not exhaustively read the ASM codegen, full serializer package, or support/* integration modules.
limitations: Static, read-only review only: no build, no tests, no scanners, no runtime or exploit verification.

The P1 relation index is partial and has no data-flow/control-flow or semantic resolution; the call trace is derived from source text and index navigation candidates, which do not prove runtime reachability.
Coverage is not exhaustive: only the parser/deserialization/config/class-loading core was reviewed in depth; ASM codegen, the serializer package, and support modules were only sampled.
One file was excluded by the harness sensitive-name/path filter and could not be inspected.
Exploitability depends on deployment-specific factors (untyped parse entry points, available gadget classes, JDK JNDI restrictions) that cannot be verified from this snapshot.
The harness refused binary-like files and does not expose git history, so the exact upstream commit/fix pairing could not be confirmed from within this run.

rejected_leads.lead: Deny-list/autoType bypass through alternate class-name forms handled in TypeUtils.loadClass (array descriptor `[...` at lines 1006-1009 and `L...;` stripping at lines 1011-1014), which can make a denied class name evade a prefix deny check.
rejected_leads.reason: This is the same root cause (no real autoType gate) and is moot here because the default deny list only blocks java.lang.Thread, so no gadget class needs bypassing; I did not split it into a second candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: MiscCodec `java.lang.Class` deserialization (serializer/MiscCodec.java lines 320-321: `TypeUtils.loadClass(strVal, ...)` driven by JSON content).
rejected_leads.reason: It loads an arbitrary class name but does not itself instantiate the class or invoke setters, so by itself it is only class-loading/info exposure and is weaker than the autoType instantiation path; kept as part of the same untrusted-type-selection theme.

rejected_leads.lead: ThrowableDeserializer honoring `@type` (parser/deserializer/ThrowableDeserializer.java lines 72-75, plus the Throwable assignability pre-check at line 45).
rejected_leads.reason: It is constrained to Throwable subclasses and is a narrower instance of the same autoType issue; no independent candidate.
No `invoke(`/`getMethod(` reflective method invocation exists in the file, and no attacker-to-sink flow for code execution was identified; not a supported candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Deny-check placement after the deserializer cache lookup in ParserConfig.getDeserializer (lines 328-340 vs 360-367) as a cache-based bypass.
rejected_leads.reason: The deny check precedes `putDeserializer`/`createJavaBeanDeserializer`, so a denied class is not registered before the check; no bypass path found, and the list is trivially weak anyway.

summary: The snapshot is fastjson 1.2.25-SNAPSHOT (pre-release, JSON.VERSION="1.2.25", pom 1.2.25-SNAPSHOT) with a partial security-denylist mechanism but without any autoType gate: no `checkAutoType`, no `autoTypeSupport`, no `Feature.SupportAutoType` (zero case-insensitive "autotype" occurrences in the tree; the relation index also has no such symbol). `DefaultJSONParser.parseObject(Map, ...)` unconditionally honors the attacker-controlled `@type` key, calls `TypeUtils.loadClass(typeName, ...)` (classloader -> context classloader -> `Class.forName`), and deserializes the resulting class; the only protection is `ParserConfig.getDeserializer`'s denyList, whose default is exactly `{"java.lang.Thread"}` (plus an empty-by-default `fastjson.parser.deny` runtime property). `JavaBeanDeserializer` then instantiates the class and `FieldDeserializer.setValue` reflectively invokes its setters with attacker values, which is the classic fastjson autoType gadget path (e.g., JDK `com.sun.rowset.JdbcRowSetImpl` `dataSourceName` + `autoCommit` -> JNDI lookup -> remote class loading). This matches CVE-2017-18349 (fixed upstream in 1.2.25 by adding the autoType switch and expanded deny list). One candidate submitted; other leads are recorded as rejected/weaker.
